questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT usually listed among the essential elements of a State?
options: A permanent population
A common religion practised by all citizens
A sovereign government
A defined territory
questions.explanation: The classical elements of a State are population, territory, government, and sovereignty; a shared religion is not a defining requirement.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Government, as a concept, is best understood as the
options: total landmass under a country's control
machinery through which the will of the State is formulated, expressed, and enforced
collection of private businesses operating in a country
sum of a country's cultural traditions
questions.explanation: Government is the institutional apparatus (legislature, executive, judiciary) that translates the State's authority into concrete laws, policies, and enforcement.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which distinguishes 'de jure' recognition of a government from 'de facto' recognition?
options: De jure recognition is full and formal legal recognition, while de facto recognition is provisional acknowledgment of effective control
De facto recognition is always granted before de jure recognition in every case
De jure recognition applies only to monarchies
There is no practical difference between the two
questions.explanation: De jure recognition confers complete legal status on a government, whereas de facto recognition merely acknowledges that a government is in actual, effective control.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 'social contract' theory of the origin of the State holds that
options: the State evolved purely from evolutionary biological instincts
the State is a divine creation with rulers appointed directly by God
the State was created solely through conquest and force
individuals voluntarily surrendered some natural freedoms to a sovereign authority in exchange for order and protection
questions.explanation: Thinkers like Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau argued that people in a 'state of nature' agreed to form government to secure peace, order, and protection of rights.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Thomas Hobbes described life in the state of nature as
options: peaceful, cooperative, and abundant
organised under an elected council
governed by natural moral law without conflict
solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short
questions.explanation: In 'Leviathan', Hobbes argued that without a strong central authority, human life in the state of nature would be marked by constant conflict and insecurity.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: According to John Locke, the primary purpose of government is to
options: maximise the personal wealth of the ruler
ensure permanent one-party rule
eliminate all forms of private property
protect the natural rights of life, liberty, and property
questions.explanation: Locke's social contract theory held that people form government chiefly to safeguard natural rights they already possess, especially life, liberty, and property.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 'force theory' of the origin of the State suggests that the State emerged mainly through
options: voluntary agreement among equals
gradual evolution of the family unit
divine appointment of rulers
conquest and the subjugation of weaker groups by stronger ones
questions.explanation: The force theory argues that early states were formed when stronger groups or individuals conquered and dominated weaker ones, imposing rule by strength.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which best defines 'political ideology'?
options: A treaty between two neighbouring states
A coherent set of ideas and beliefs about how society and government should be organised
A single law passed by a legislature
A country's official national anthem
questions.explanation: A political ideology is a structured system of beliefs (e.g. liberalism, socialism, conservatism) guiding views on the proper organisation of government and society.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Communism, in its classical Marxist sense, envisions a society characterised by
options: a classless, stateless society with common ownership of the means of production
unregulated private capital accumulation
rule by a hereditary monarch
strict hereditary class divisions maintained by law
questions.explanation: Marxist communism envisages the eventual abolition of class distinctions and private ownership of productive resources, replaced by communal ownership.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Liberalism, as a political ideology, places the greatest emphasis on
options: the abolition of private property
rule by a single dominant political party
total state control of the economy
individual liberty, limited government, and protection of civil rights
questions.explanation: Classical liberalism prioritises individual freedoms, constitutionally limited government power, and the protection of civil and property rights.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes 'power' from 'influence' in politics?
options: Power and influence are exactly the same thing
Power involves the capacity to compel obedience, while influence involves persuading others without direct coercion
Influence always requires the use of physical force
Power can only be exercised by elected officials
questions.explanation: Power often carries an element of compulsion or sanction, whereas influence relies on persuasion, respect, or example rather than coercive enforcement.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A theocracy is a system of government in which
options: power is inherited through a purely secular royal bloodline
power rests solely with the military
the people directly vote on every governmental decision
political authority is claimed to derive from and be exercised according to religious law
questions.explanation: In a theocracy, governance is conducted in the name of a deity, typically through religious leaders applying religious law as the basis of political authority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Totalitarianism is best described as a system in which
options: the State seeks to control virtually all aspects of public and private life
power is strictly limited by a written bill of rights
multiple political parties compete freely for office
local governments are fully independent of the centre
questions.explanation: Totalitarian regimes attempt near-total control over political, economic, social, and even private aspects of citizens' lives, often through a single dominant party.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In a direct democracy, as practised in ancient Athens, political decisions were made
options: by military officers appointed for life
by a single monarch after consulting priests
exclusively by a hereditary council of elders
by eligible citizens voting personally on issues rather than through elected representatives
questions.explanation: Direct democracy involves citizens participating personally in lawmaking and decision-making, as opposed to representative democracy where elected officials decide on their behalf.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Representative democracy differs from direct democracy mainly because
options: it eliminates the need for a constitution
citizens elect officials to make decisions on their behalf rather than voting on every issue themselves
it restricts voting rights to only wealthy citizens
it does not require any elections at all
questions.explanation: Representative democracy, the dominant modern form, has citizens choose representatives who then deliberate and legislate on their behalf.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of these is a key feature distinguishing a federal system from a unitary one?
options: The total elimination of local governments
The permanent suspension of elections
The existence of a written constitution that constitutionally guarantees powers to constituent states
The complete absence of any national government
questions.explanation: Federal systems require a rigid, written constitution that entrenches the division of powers between the centre and constituent units, protecting each from unilateral encroachment.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following countries operates a federal system of government, like Nigeria?
options: France
Japan
the United Kingdom
The United States of America
questions.explanation: Like Nigeria, the USA constitutionally divides power between a federal government and constituent states, unlike the largely unitary systems of France, the UK, and Japan.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: One major advantage of a federal system of government is that it
options: eliminates the possibility of disputes between different levels of government
allows for the accommodation of diverse ethnic, cultural, or regional groups within one country
guarantees the fastest possible decision-making at all times
removes the need for a central government entirely
questions.explanation: Federalism allows regions with distinct identities or interests to retain a measure of self-governance while remaining united under one country, easing diversity management.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key disadvantage often associated with federalism is that it can lead to
options: instant uniformity of laws across the whole country
the complete absence of any regional identity
duplication of institutions and possible friction between federal and state governments
the total elimination of a national army
questions.explanation: Because power and institutions exist at both federal and state levels, federal systems can experience costly duplication and jurisdictional conflicts.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In a parliamentary system such as the United Kingdom's, the Head of Government is typically
options: a President directly elected by the entire electorate
the Prime Minister, chosen from the majority party or coalition in Parliament
a monarch who personally directs day-to-day policy
an appointed council of unelected technocrats
questions.explanation: In parliamentary systems, the Prime Minister emerges from the legislature (usually the leader of the majority party) and remains accountable to it.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under Nigeria's presidential system since 1979 and 1999, the President is
options: both Head of State and Head of Government, elected independently of the National Assembly
elected by members of the National Assembly
subordinate to the Senate President in matters of state
merely a ceremonial figure with no executive powers
questions.explanation: Nigeria's presidential model, adopted from the USA, fuses the roles of Head of State and Head of Government in one directly elected President.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best describes 'constitutional monarchy'?
options: A system where a monarch serves as ceremonial Head of State while real political power lies with elected officials
A system with no monarch or elected officials at all
A system where the monarch is elected by popular vote every four years
A system where the monarch exercises absolute, unchecked power
questions.explanation: In constitutional monarchies like the UK, the monarch's role is largely symbolic, while a Prime Minister and Parliament exercise actual governing authority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An absolute monarchy differs from a constitutional monarchy chiefly in that in an absolute monarchy
options: the head of state is chosen by direct popular election
the monarch holds unchecked, unlimited political power
the monarch has purely ceremonial functions
power is shared equally between the monarch and an elected parliament
questions.explanation: Unlike constitutional monarchs restrained by law and parliament, absolute monarchs exercise supreme, largely unrestrained authority over the state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Judicial review refers to the power of the courts to
options: draft new legislation for the National Assembly
examine and nullify laws or executive actions found to be inconsistent with the constitution
appoint members of the executive cabinet
declare war on behalf of the State
questions.explanation: Judicial review empowers courts to strike down laws or government actions that violate the constitution, reinforcing the judiciary's checking role over the other arms.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best illustrates a legislative check on the executive?
options: The power of the legislature to impeach or remove an erring president
The executive's power to propose a budget
The judiciary's power to interpret statutes
The president's power to appoint judges
questions.explanation: Impeachment is a classic legislative check, allowing the legislature to remove a president or other officials for gross misconduct, restraining executive excess.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The power of the executive to veto a bill passed by the legislature is an example of
options: an executive check on the legislature
a legislative check on the judiciary
an unconstitutional abuse of power
a judicial check on the executive
questions.explanation: A presidential veto allows the executive to reject legislation, serving as a constitutional check that can, in turn, often be overridden by a legislative supermajority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A unicameral legislature, unlike a bicameral one, consists of
options: three separate chambers
two equal legislative chambers
no formal legislative chamber
a single legislative chamber
questions.explanation: Unicameral legislatures have only one chamber, contrasting with bicameral legislatures (like Nigeria's National Assembly) that have two, such as a Senate and House.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In Nigeria's National Assembly, the Senate is composed of how many senators, three from each state and one from the Federal Capital Territory?
questions.explanation: Nigeria's Senate has 109 members: three senators from each of the 36 states plus one representing the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The principle of the 'independence of the judiciary' primarily requires that
options: the judiciary should have no relationship whatsoever with the other arms of government
the judiciary should control the national budget
judges should be free from undue influence or interference by the executive or legislature in deciding cases
judges should be elected directly by popular vote
questions.explanation: Judicial independence ensures courts can adjudicate impartially, insulated from political pressure by the executive or legislative branches, safeguarding the rule of law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a key function of the Executive arm of government besides law enforcement?
options: Interpreting statutes in individual court cases
Enacting bills into law
Formulating and implementing government policy
Ratifying constitutional amendments through referenda alone
questions.explanation: Beyond enforcing laws, the executive is also responsible for shaping and implementing broad government policy across sectors like the economy, defence, and welfare.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An 'ombudsman', where such an office exists, is primarily responsible for
options: investigating citizens' complaints against maladministration by government agencies
prosecuting criminal offences in court
commanding the national armed forces
drafting the national budget
questions.explanation: An ombudsman serves as an independent watchdog investigating and addressing citizen grievances relating to unfair or improper conduct by public bodies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The power of 'confirmation' exercised by the Nigerian Senate over certain presidential appointees is an example of
options: a purely ceremonial function with no real effect
a judicial check on legislative powers
an executive check on judicial appointments
a legislative check on executive appointment powers
questions.explanation: By vetting and confirming key presidential nominees (such as ministers), the Senate exercises oversight that checks unrestrained executive appointment power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which arm of government is primarily responsible for the 'power of the purse' in most democracies, including Nigeria?
options: The Judiciary, through constitutional interpretation
The Executive alone, without any oversight
The Legislature, through its power to approve or reject the budget
The traditional council of chiefs
questions.explanation: The legislature's authority to scrutinise, amend, and approve government spending (the 'power of the purse') is a fundamental check on executive financial power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Citizenship by registration, under the 1999 Nigerian Constitution, is typically available to
options: any foreigner who has merely visited Nigeria on a tourist visa
a woman who is or has been married to a Nigerian citizen, among other qualifying persons
only persons born outside Nigeria to non-Nigerian parents
persons who have never resided in Nigeria
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution allows certain categories, including a woman married to a Nigerian citizen, to acquire Nigerian citizenship through registration.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Citizenship by naturalisation in Nigeria generally requires a foreigner to
options: simply declare an intention to become Nigerian with no residency requirement
have resided in Nigeria for a specified minimum period and satisfy other statutory conditions
be born in Nigeria to Nigerian parents
be married to a Nigerian citizen for less than one year
questions.explanation: Naturalisation requires the applicant to meet conditions such as continuous residency, good character, and adequate knowledge of a Nigerian language.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes 'human rights' from ordinary legal rights?
options: Human rights are granted exclusively by the legislature
Human rights apply only to citizens of a particular country
Human rights can be freely revoked by any government at will
Human rights are inherent and belong to every person by virtue of being human, regardless of citizenship
questions.explanation: Human rights are considered universal and inalienable, attaching to all persons by virtue of their humanity, unlike rights created purely by domestic statute.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of these is classified as a fundamental human right under Chapter IV of the 1999 Nigerian Constitution?
options: Right to fair hearing
Right to unlimited government subsidy
Right to a government job
Right to free housing for every citizen
questions.explanation: Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution guarantees justiciable fundamental rights such as the right to life, dignity, personal liberty, and fair hearing.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The rights contained in Chapter II of the 1999 Nigerian Constitution, dealing with Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy, are
options: fully enforceable in the same way as fundamental rights in Chapter IV
non-justiciable, meaning they cannot ordinarily be enforced directly in court
applicable only to foreign nationals residing in Nigeria
reserved exclusively for members of the armed forces
questions.explanation: Unlike Chapter IV rights, the socio-economic objectives in Chapter II are directive principles that guide governance but are generally not directly enforceable in court.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A 'stateless person' is best described as someone who
options: has renounced citizenship voluntarily but retains full legal protection everywhere
is not recognised as a citizen or national by any country under its laws
holds dual citizenship in two countries
is a refugee who automatically becomes a citizen of the host country
questions.explanation: Statelessness occurs when an individual lacks recognised nationality anywhere, often leaving them without the legal protections citizenship normally confers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a civic duty of a citizen, as opposed to a civic right?
options: Freedom of expression
Obeying the laws of the land
Right to vote
Right to own property
questions.explanation: While voting, expression, and property ownership are rights citizens enjoy, obedience to law is a corresponding civic duty citizens owe the State.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Dual citizenship refers to a situation where a person
options: holds only temporary residency status in a foreign country
is a citizen of a country but resides permanently abroad
has been stripped of citizenship in every country
simultaneously holds recognised citizenship of two different countries
questions.explanation: Dual citizenship means an individual is legally recognised as a citizen of two countries at the same time, each with its own attendant rights and obligations.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under Nigerian law, citizenship may be revoked from a naturalised or registered citizen mainly on grounds such as
options: disloyalty or engaging in acts prejudicial to national security
having attended a foreign university
residing outside Nigeria for a short holiday
practising a minority religion
questions.explanation: The Constitution permits deprivation of citizenship acquired by registration or naturalisation on grounds like disloyalty, fraud in acquisition, or acts against national interest.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The right to vote and be voted for in Nigeria is generally referred to as
options: cultural right
political right
social right
economic right
questions.explanation: Rights that enable citizens to participate in governance, such as voting and contesting elections, are classified as political rights.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A political party is best defined as an organisation that
options: seeks to gain political power by contesting elections and forming or influencing government
is formed only during a period of military rule
operates strictly as a private commercial enterprise
exists solely to provide charity to its members
questions.explanation: Political parties exist primarily to win elections and control the machinery of government in order to implement their programmes and policies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best describes a 'multi-party system'?
options: A system with exactly two dominant parties and no others
A system with no political parties whatsoever
A system permitting only one legally recognised party
A political system in which more than two parties genuinely compete for political power
questions.explanation: A multi-party system, common in many democracies, features three or more parties with a realistic chance of winning power or influencing government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An electoral college, as used in some countries, is a body that
options: manages foreign diplomatic missions abroad
formally elects a head of state or government on behalf of the general electorate
supervises university admission examinations
reviews and approves proposed constitutional amendments only
questions.explanation: In systems using an electoral college (e.g. the USA), designated electors formally cast the votes that determine the outcome of a presidential election, based on the popular vote.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) in Nigeria is primarily responsible for
options: appointing state governors after elections
prosecuting persons accused of electoral offences in the Supreme Court
organising and conducting elections and registering voters and political parties
commanding security agencies during elections
questions.explanation: INEC is Nigeria's independent electoral management body, tasked with voter registration, party registration, and the conduct of elections at federal and state levels.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best describes 'gerrymandering'?
options: The formal announcement of election results by an electoral commission
A method of educating first-time voters
The practice of counting ballots publicly in front of observers
The manipulation of electoral constituency boundaries to favour a particular party or group
questions.explanation: Gerrymandering involves deliberately redrawing electoral district boundaries to give one political group an unfair advantage in elections.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: 'Universal adult suffrage' means that
options: voting rights are restricted to landowners
only university graduates are permitted to vote
only male citizens are entitled to vote
all adult citizens who meet basic legal requirements have the right to vote, regardless of class, gender, or wealth
questions.explanation: Universal adult suffrage extends the right to vote broadly to all qualifying adult citizens, without discrimination based on gender, property, or social class.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which best explains the term 'pressure group' in the political process?
options: An arm of government responsible for tax collection
A branch of the armed forces responsible for internal security
A political party that has won a general election
An organised group that seeks to influence government policy without directly seeking to win elections or hold public office
questions.explanation: Unlike political parties, pressure (or interest) groups aim to influence government decisions and policy from outside, without contesting elections to hold office themselves.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A referendum is best described as
options: the process by which a legislature debates a bill
a direct vote by citizens on a specific political issue, such as a proposed constitutional change
a system for selecting party delegates at a convention
a method by which judges are appointed
questions.explanation: A referendum allows citizens to directly decide a specific issue by ballot, rather than leaving the decision solely to elected representatives.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The term 'floating voters' refers to voters who
options: are permanently registered to vote in more than one constituency
do not have a fixed allegiance to any particular political party and may change their vote between elections
have been legally disqualified from voting
vote only in local government elections
questions.explanation: Floating voters lack strong, consistent party loyalty, making them a key target for parties seeking to swing election outcomes.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best describes 'political apathy'?
options: A legal requirement to vote in every election
Active membership in multiple political parties simultaneously
Strong enthusiasm and high turnout in elections
A general lack of interest or participation by citizens in political processes such as voting
questions.explanation: Political apathy describes indifference toward political participation, often reflected in low voter turnout and disengagement from civic processes.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An electoral system based on 'proportional representation' allocates legislative seats
options: entirely to the single candidate with the most votes in each constituency
roughly in proportion to the share of votes each party receives
equally to every registered political party regardless of votes received
solely based on the population of the capital city
questions.explanation: Proportional representation systems try to align a party's share of seats closely with its share of the total votes cast, unlike winner-take-all constituency systems.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's electoral system for most elections is best described as
options: a system with no elections, only appointments
a pure proportional representation system
an electoral college system
a simple majority (first-past-the-post) system
questions.explanation: Nigeria largely uses a first-past-the-post system, in which the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, without needing an absolute majority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Civil Service is best defined as the body of officials who
options: are appointed exclusively to political party leadership positions
are elected periodically to make laws
implement government policy and administer public affairs on a permanent, professional, and politically neutral basis
serve only in the armed forces
questions.explanation: Civil servants form the permanent bureaucratic machinery that implements government policy, remaining professionally neutral irrespective of which party is in power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of an ideal civil service?
options: Direct involvement in partisan election campaigns
Automatic loss of office whenever a new government is elected
Political neutrality in carrying out official duties
Total exemption from any code of conduct
questions.explanation: A core principle of civil service is political neutrality, enabling officials to serve any government of the day impartially and professionally.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: 'Public corporations' in Nigeria, such as the Nigerian National Petroleum Company, are typically established to
options: serve exclusively as political party fundraising bodies
compete purely for private shareholder profit with no public accountability
provide essential services or manage strategic sectors of the economy on behalf of the State
replace the functions of the legislature
questions.explanation: Public corporations are set up by government, often by statute, to run essential services or strategic industries that serve broad public interest.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Decentralisation in public administration refers to the
options: transfer of administrative authority from a central government to lower levels of government or agencies
replacement of civilian administrators with military officers
concentration of all administrative power at the centre
complete abolition of a central government
questions.explanation: Decentralisation disperses decision-making and administrative powers away from the centre to regional, state, or local bodies, improving responsiveness to local needs.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: 'Bureaucracy', in Max Weber's classical sense, is characterised chiefly by
options: a hierarchical structure with clearly defined rules, roles, and procedures
the total absence of any formal rules or hierarchy
decisions made purely on personal favouritism rather than rules
temporary staff who serve for only a few days at a time
questions.explanation: Weber described ideal bureaucracy as organised around formal rules, a clear hierarchy of authority, defined roles, and impersonal, rule-based decision-making.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Local government, as the third tier of government in Nigeria, primarily exists to
options: conduct Nigeria's foreign policy
replace the need for state governments entirely
control the national armed forces
bring governance and basic services closer to the grassroots population
questions.explanation: Local government is designed to decentralise governance to the community level, delivering services like primary healthcare, local roads, and markets directly to residents.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a major function typically assigned to local governments under the Nigerian Constitution?
options: Negotiation of international treaties
Declaration of war on other countries
Construction and maintenance of local roads, streets, and markets
Issuance of national currency
questions.explanation: The Fourth Schedule of the 1999 Constitution assigns local governments functions such as local roads, markets, and primary healthcare, among others.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: 'Public accountability' in government administration primarily means that
options: public officials must answer for how they exercise authority and use public resources
only elected officials, and not civil servants, can be held responsible
financial records of government agencies should remain permanently confidential
government officials are exempt from any form of scrutiny
questions.explanation: Accountability requires that those entrusted with public power and resources be answerable to the public, typically through audits, oversight, and reporting mechanisms.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 'Federal Character Principle' in Nigeria's public service is designed mainly to
options: restrict public service employment to a single ethnic group
abolish the civil service entirely
ensure fair representation of Nigeria's diverse states and ethnic groups in public appointments
give automatic preference to foreign nationals in public jobs
questions.explanation: The Federal Character Principle, entrenched in the 1999 Constitution, seeks to reflect Nigeria's federal diversity in public sector appointments and reduce ethnic or sectional domination.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best describes 'privatisation' as a public administration policy?
options: The nationalisation of previously private businesses
The abolition of all taxation
The creation of new government ministries
The transfer of ownership or management of public enterprises to private individuals or companies
questions.explanation: Privatisation involves shifting state-owned enterprises into private hands, often to improve efficiency, reduce fiscal burden, and encourage competition.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The pre-colonial Oyo Empire's political system was notably characterised by
options: a centralised monarchy headed by the Alaafin, checked by the Oyo Mesi council of chiefs
a completely stateless, decentralised society with no central authority
government by an elected national assembly
direct rule by British colonial residents
questions.explanation: The Oyo Empire had a centralised monarchy under the Alaafin, whose powers were constitutionally checked by the Oyo Mesi, a council of powerful chieftains.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In the pre-colonial Oyo political system, the Bashorun was significant primarily because he
options: headed the Oyo Mesi and could, on behalf of the council, compel an unpopular Alaafin to commit suicide
was the supreme religious head of the Yoruba pantheon
commanded the British colonial police force
presided over Islamic courts in Oyo
questions.explanation: As head of the Oyo Mesi, the Bashorun wielded immense power, including the symbolic authority to reject an unpopular Alaafin by presenting him with an empty calabash or parrot's eggs, signalling he must take his own life.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The pre-colonial Igbo political system is typically described as
options: administered directly by British colonial governors
a highly centralised empire ruled by a single hereditary emperor
largely stateless and republican, with authority diffused among councils of elders, age-grades, and title societies
governed by an absolute theocratic monarch
questions.explanation: Unlike centralised kingdoms, most pre-colonial Igbo communities lacked a single paramount ruler; authority was instead shared among elders, age-grades, and title-holding societies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Among the pre-colonial Igbo, the 'Ozo' title society functioned mainly as
options: a body exclusively responsible for tax collection under British rule
a religious sect banned from political participation
an armed police force enforcing colonial law
a group of accomplished, respected men who exercised significant social and political influence in the community
questions.explanation: The Ozo title conferred prestige and political influence on accomplished men, who played key advisory and decision-making roles in community governance.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The pre-colonial Benin Kingdom was governed by
options: a council of elected representatives with no monarch
a loosely organised confederation of stateless villages
British colonial administrators from its founding
an Oba who wielded centralised authority, supported by a hierarchy of palace and town chiefs
questions.explanation: The Benin Kingdom had a highly centralised monarchy under the Oba, whose authority was administered through structured palace chiefs (Uzama) and town chiefs.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Sokoto Caliphate, founded after Usman dan Fodio's jihad, was organised as
options: a colony directly administered by the British Crown
a stateless society without any central ruler
a centralised Islamic theocratic empire administered through emirates under a Sultan
a purely secular federation of independent city-states
questions.explanation: The Sokoto Caliphate was a highly organised Islamic empire, with power centralised under the Sultan (Caliph) and delegated to Emirs governing constituent emirates.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under the Sokoto Caliphate system, an Emir's authority over his emirate was primarily derived from
options: hereditary succession with no reference to the Sultan
direct election by the general population of the emirate
a flag (turban) of investiture conferred by the Sultan of Sokoto, symbolising delegated authority
appointment by British colonial governors
questions.explanation: Emirs derived legitimacy from the Sultan of Sokoto, who conferred a flag of investiture symbolising the delegation of religious and political authority to govern the emirate.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of these best describes a common feature of stateless societies in pre-colonial Nigeria, such as many Igbo and Tiv communities?
options: All political power was held by one hereditary king
Authority was exercised exclusively by colonial-appointed warrant chiefs
Political authority was diffused rather than concentrated in a single central ruler
Governance was conducted solely through a written constitution
questions.explanation: Stateless societies lacked a single overarching ruler; instead, governance was distributed among kinship groups, age-grades, and councils of elders.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The age-grade system, common in many pre-colonial Nigerian societies, functioned mainly to
options: replace the need for any council of elders
act as the judicial arm under British colonial rule
serve as the sole religious authority in the community
organise people of similar age into groups responsible for specific communal duties, including defence and public works
questions.explanation: Age-grades grouped community members by age cohort, assigning them collective responsibilities such as community labour, security, and social discipline.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Yoruba Oyo Mesi council traditionally comprised how many principal chiefs, headed by the Bashorun?
options: Twelve
Twenty
Three
Seven
questions.explanation: The Oyo Mesi was traditionally composed of seven principal chiefs, headed by the Bashorun, serving as a check on the Alaafin's power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Indirect rule, as applied by the British in colonial Nigeria, was a system in which
options: Nigeria was granted full self-government immediately after conquest
traditional rulers were completely abolished and replaced by British officials
colonial power was exercised solely through the Nigerian judiciary
colonial administration was carried out through existing traditional rulers and institutions under British supervision
questions.explanation: Indirect rule, associated with Lord Lugard, governed through existing traditional authorities (emirs, obas, chiefs) who implemented British colonial policy at the local level.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Indirect rule was applied most successfully in Northern Nigeria mainly because
options: Northern Nigeria had no traditional rulers at all
Northern communities rejected any form of traditional authority
the British abolished all existing emirates before introducing the system
the existing Sokoto Caliphate structure provided a ready centralised hierarchy the British could work through
questions.explanation: The North's centralised emirate system, with clear hierarchical authority under emirs, fit neatly into the British model of ruling indirectly through existing structures.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key challenge in applying indirect rule to stateless societies in Eastern Nigeria was that
options: the British found willing central emperors to negotiate with
these societies already had a monarchy identical to that of the North
these societies lacked a centralised chieftaincy structure the British could readily use, leading to the imposition of 'warrant chiefs'
there was no British presence at all in Eastern Nigeria
questions.explanation: Because many Igbo communities were stateless, the British artificially imposed 'warrant chiefs' with no traditional legitimacy, which fuelled later unrest such as the Aba Women's Riot of 1929.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Aba Women's Riot of 1929 was primarily a protest against
options: the introduction of Western education
the warrant chief system and the imposition of taxation on women
the granting of Nigerian independence
the establishment of the Sokoto Caliphate
questions.explanation: The 1929 uprising was sparked by fears that colonial authorities, through warrant chiefs, intended to tax women, compounding resentment against the illegitimate warrant chief system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Lord Frederick Lugard is most closely associated with which colonial policy in Nigeria?
options: The system of Indirect Rule
The founding of the Sokoto Caliphate
Nigeria's independence constitution
The introduction of a fully elective legislature
questions.explanation: Lord Lugard, first Governor-General of the amalgamated Nigeria, is best known for developing and applying the policy of Indirect Rule.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates of Nigeria took place in the year
questions.explanation: Lord Lugard oversaw the amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates into a single colony and protectorate of Nigeria in 1914.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 is significant chiefly because it
options: granted Nigeria full independence
introduced the elective principle into Nigerian politics for the first time, allowing limited elections to the Legislative Council
abolished the Legislative Council entirely
created Nigeria's first three regions
questions.explanation: The Clifford Constitution allowed Lagos and Calabar to elect a small number of members to the Legislative Council, marking the first taste of elective representation in Nigeria.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Richards Constitution of 1946 is best remembered for
options: abolishing the office of Governor-General
creating a fully federal system with twelve states
introducing regionalism by dividing Nigeria into three regions: North, East, and West
granting Nigeria full independence from Britain
questions.explanation: The Richards Constitution divided Nigeria into three regions, laying the institutional groundwork for the federalism that would later develop more fully.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 is notable for
options: abolishing all regional governments
expanding regional legislative powers and increasing Nigerian participation in central government
introducing Nigeria's first republican constitution
establishing Nigeria as a military dictatorship
questions.explanation: The Macpherson Constitution deepened regional autonomy and expanded Nigerian representation, though its central legislature structure soon proved unworkable, prompting further review.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 is significant mainly because it
options: granted Nigeria's outright independence
formally established Nigeria as a federation of three regions with a strong central government
abolished the position of regional premiers
reunited the Northern and Southern Protectorates for the first time
questions.explanation: The Lyttleton Constitution entrenched federalism, formally structuring Nigeria into three regions (North, East, West) each with considerable self-government, under a federal centre.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria gained independence from British colonial rule on
options: 1 October 1960
15 January 1966
1 October 1963
questions.explanation: Nigeria became an independent nation on 1 October 1960, though it remained a constitutional monarchy under the British Crown until 1963.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria became a republic, replacing the British monarch with an indigenous President as Head of State, on
options: 31 December 1983
1 October 1979
1 October 1963
1 October 1960
questions.explanation: On 1 October 1963, Nigeria adopted a republican constitution, becoming the Federal Republic of Nigeria with Nnamdi Azikiwe as its first President.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's first Prime Minister under the 1960 Independence Constitution was
options: Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe
Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa
Chief Obafemi Awolowo
General Yakubu Gowon
questions.explanation: Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa served as Nigeria's Prime Minister, the head of government, from independence in 1960 until the January 1966 coup.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under the 1963 Republican Constitution, the ceremonial position of Head of State was held by
options: the President
the Senate President
the Prime Minister
the Governor-General
questions.explanation: The 1963 Constitution replaced the Governor-General (a representative of the British Crown) with an indigenous President as ceremonial Head of State, while the Prime Minister remained Head of Government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1979 Constitution marked a fundamental departure from Nigeria's earlier constitutions mainly because it
options: introduced the American-style presidential system, replacing the Westminster parliamentary model
reintroduced colonial rule
restored the parliamentary system of government
abolished the federal system entirely
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution replaced the earlier Westminster-style parliamentary system with a US-inspired presidential system, fusing the roles of Head of State and Head of Government in an elected President.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Alhaji Shehu Shagari became Nigeria's first executive President under the 1979 Constitution, taking office in
questions.explanation: Shehu Shagari was elected as Nigeria's first executive President under the 1979 Constitution, inaugurating the Second Republic on 1 October 1979.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria came into effect on
options: 1 October 1999
31 December 1983
12 June 1993
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution took effect on 29 May 1999, marking the transition to civilian rule under President Olusegun Obasanjo and the start of the Fourth Republic.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 12 June 1993 presidential election, widely believed to have been won by Chief MKO Abiola, is significant because it was
options: won decisively by a military candidate
the first election held under the 1999 Constitution
the first election in which women could vote in Nigeria
annulled by the military government of General Ibrahim Babangida
questions.explanation: The 12 June 1993 election, seen as one of Nigeria's freest, was annulled by the Babangida administration, triggering a major political crisis and prolonged agitation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best describes a major structural feature introduced or entrenched by the 1999 Constitution?
options: Rule by a Governor-General representing the British monarch
A single-party political system
A presidential system with a bicameral National Assembly and 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory
A unicameral parliament with no states
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution retains the presidential model, a bicameral National Assembly (Senate and House of Representatives), and a federation of 36 states plus the FCT.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1989 Constitution, drafted under General Ibrahim Babangida but never fully implemented nationally, was intended to introduce
options: the abolition of the office of President
an absolute monarchy
a two-party political system (the SDP and NRC) designed by the military government
a return to the parliamentary system
questions.explanation: The Babangida transition programme created and mandated only two government-designed parties, the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and National Republican Convention (NRC).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's first military coup, which toppled the First Republic, took place in
options: July 1966
October 1960
December 1983
January 1966
questions.explanation: The 15 January 1966 coup, led by a group of majors, overthrew the civilian government and installed Major-General Aguiyi-Ironsi as Head of State, ending the First Republic.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Major-General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi's Unification Decree No. 34 of 1966 is significant because it
options: attempted to replace Nigeria's federal structure with a unitary system of government
reinstated the 1963 Republican Constitution unchanged
granted Nigeria's independence from Britain
created the twelve-state structure
questions.explanation: Decree No. 34 sought to abolish regionalism in favour of a unitary government, a move that provoked strong opposition, particularly in the North, and contributed to the July 1966 counter-coup.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The counter-coup of July 1966 resulted in the emergence of which military Head of State?
options: General Ibrahim Babangida
General Yakubu Gowon
General Muhammadu Buhari
General Sani Abacha
questions.explanation: The July 1966 counter-coup brought Lieutenant-Colonel Yakubu Gowon to power as Head of State, following the killing of General Aguiyi-Ironsi.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Nigerian Civil War, fought between the federal government and the secessionist Republic of Biafra, lasted from
questions.explanation: The civil war began in July 1967, after the Eastern Region under Lieutenant-Colonel Odumegwu Ojukwu declared independence as Biafra, and ended in January 1970.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: General Yakubu Gowon's creation of twelve states in 1967 was intended primarily to
options: reunite Nigeria with Britain
establish a permanent one-party state
abolish the federal system entirely
weaken the appeal of secession by breaking up the old regions, including the Eastern Region
questions.explanation: By subdividing the four regions into twelve states, Gowon aimed to satisfy minority demands and undercut the Eastern Region's unified base for secession.
